rashi:a2.1: What are they? Two categories: it now occurs to us that black and white ones are also like two kinds. And if Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri also, like Rabbi Yehuda, set their dispute where one intended to pick this one and picked that one, what does Rabbi Yehuda come to teach us?
tosafot:a2.1: This is the same as Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri: for you must say that this is the meaning of their statement: “They did not disagree about a matter of one category, that he is liable,” such as figs and figs where the picker lost his train of thought, or white and white, or black and black, where the picker lost his train of thought, as explained above; “about what did they disagree? About a matter of two categories,” such as grapes or figs, or black and white, where the picker lost his train of thought, as their reason is explained above. For we cannot say that according to Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri “about what did they disagree? About a matter of two categories” means a case where he picked figs or grapes and does not know what he picked, for what would that teach us?
rashi:a3.1: Rather, is it not that acting unawares is the difference between them: Rabbi Yehuda heard Rabbi Shimon Shezuri set the dispute where the picker lost his train of thought, while with one who acts unawares all agree he is exempt; and he came to say that even “he intended to pick,” etc., is acting unawares, and since they acted unawares with a prohibited matter, they disagree: Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable, and even Rabbi Yehoshua exempted only in two categories, but in one category he is liable. And “I wonder,” etc. [as Rabbi Yehuda continues in the mishna]. “If so, why is ‘wherein’ stated?” To exclude one who acts unawares with something permitted, or one who acts unawares with one primary category of labor and performs another primary category of labor.
tosafot:a3.1:
Rather, is it not that acting unawares is the difference between them, as Rabbi Yehuda holds that one who acts unawares is liable, and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and Rabbi Shimon hold that one who acts unawares is exempt: And Rabbi Shimon holds that the dispute of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer is where the picker lost his train of thought and intended to pick figs and picked grapes, or black ones and picked white ones, which are two kinds, as their reason is explained above. But in one kind where the picker lost his train of thought they did not disagree, for all agree he is liable; while in one kind where the picker did not lose his train of thought, such as where he intended to pick these and picked others, he is exempt because he is acting unawares. And Rabbi Yehuda said: even where he intended, etc., and their dispute is in two kinds where the picker did not lose his train of thought. And from this we infer: specifically in two kinds, but in one kind all agree he is liable, as the Gemara inferred above. But why? It is acting unawares! And our difficulty returns to its place.
And the reason the Gemara takes this approach as obvious, that according to Rabbi Shimon one who acts unawares is exempt and he sets their dispute where the picker lost his train of thought, while according to Rabbi Yehuda one who acts unawares is liable and he speaks of where the picker did not lose it, is that this is what the language of the mishna implies: that Rabbi Yehuda is more stringent. For Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and Rabbi Shimon say, “They did not disagree about a matter of one category, that he is liable,” that is, there he is certainly liable; “about what did they disagree? About two categories,” etc., that is, there someone exempts. And to this Rabbi Yehuda replied: even if he intended to pick figs, etc., they disagree, and someone deems him liable. Moreover, from his saying, “I wonder if Rabbi Yehoshua exempted in this case,” it is implied that Rabbi Yehuda is more stringent.
gershom:a1.1: [A marker in the text: up to here belongs to the previous amud.] “Rather, is it not that acting unawares is the difference between them, as Rabbi Yehuda holds”: one who acts unawares in a case like this, with two kinds, is liable according to all; and that is why he says, “I wonder if Rabbi Yehoshua would exempt in this case.” But which one who acts unawares is exempt? Either as Rava [explains] or as Abaye.
gershom:a2.1: And Rabbi Shimon Shezuri holds: with one who acts unawares like this, with two kinds, Rabbi Yehoshua exempted. Thus they disagree about one who acts unawares on Shabbat, and this is difficult for Shmuel, who said that with one who acts unawares on Shabbat all agree he is exempt.
rashi:a4.1: The picker lost his train of thought, in one category: he intended this fig, and forgot, and thought, “It is another fig next to it that I want,” and his hand went to the first one. All agree he is liable, since that is what he intended at first; and moreover, when he forgot his thought, he thought only of the same kind.
gershom:a3.1: No: with one who acts unawares, all agree he is exempt, and here they disagree about this: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri holds that where the picker lost his train of thought in one category, such as two vines, and he intended to pick one, and forgot the one he had in mind to pick, and thought that it was the other he wanted to pick, and when he went to pick the one he now thought of, his hand went to the first, which he had intended earlier, all agree he is liable, since it is one kind and his intention was carried out.
rashi:a5.1: In two categories: he intended figs, and forgot, and thought, “It is grapes that I want,” and his hand went to the figs.
rashi:a5.2: And Rabbi Yehuda holds: they disagree even in one category, and he holds that black and white ones are one category, since they are one kind. (Tosafot:) What he says in the mishna, “I wonder if Rabbi Yehoshua exempted in this case,” is in one kind, since his thought was fulfilled. Up to here, Tosafot. [This bracketed Tosafot stands within Rashi’s text.]
gershom:a4.1: When they disagree, it is in two categories, two kinds: Rabbi Eliezer holds that where the picker lost his train of thought with two kinds he is liable, since his intention was carried out; and Rabbi Yehoshua exempts, since he holds that his wish and thought were not carried out. And Rabbi Yehuda holds: there is no difference between one category and a matter of two categories, they disagree, for Rabbi Yehoshua exempts even in one category. And this is how he explains the mishna:
gershom:a5.1: “Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says: They did not disagree,” etc. “About what did they disagree?” About one who lost his train of thought with two kinds, where Rabbi Eliezer, etc. And Rabbi Yehuda holds that Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable in one category, and even if he intended to pick figs, etc., which is two categories, even so he deems him liable. And Rabbi Yehoshua, who disagrees and exempts in two categories, likewise disagrees in one category and exempts. And Rabbi Yehuda says: even so, though I say that he disagrees in both, I wonder if Rabbi Yehoshua would exempt in this case, where the picker lost his train of thought with two kinds, and all the more so I wonder that he exempts in one category. Rabbi (Yehoshua) [Shimon] said to him: Do not wonder, for this is the reason that Rabbi Yehoshua exempts: because it is written, “wherein he has sinned,” excluding one who acts unawares, and this one, who lost his train of thought with two kinds, is acting unawares, since his wish and thought were not carried out. But with ordinary acting unawares on Shabbat, all agree he is exempt.
rashi:a6.1: Doing first is the difference between them: he intended to pick this one first and afterward that one, and his hand went to the latter. Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri hold: if of one category, all agree he is liable, since they are one category and in the end he did both, and we do not mind that he did first what was to be later. When they disagree, it is in two categories: Rabbi Eliezer imposes a sin offering, since he intended both and did both, and we do not mind that he did first what was to be later; and Rabbi Yehoshua exempts, since at the time of picking each one he was not intending that one, so it is acting unawares and he is exempt. And Rabbi Yehuda holds that they disagree even in one category, but “I wonder why he exempted,” since in the end he intended both. But with plain acting unawares, where he intended only one and did not do it but did the other, all agree he is exempt.
gershom:a6.1: Rava said: Doing first is the difference between them: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri holds that in a matter of two categories, if he intended to pick one before the other, and he went ahead and picked the other first, Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable and Rabbi Yehoshua exempts. And Rabbi Yehuda said: I wonder if Rabbi Yehoshua would exempt one who does first, for Rabbi Yehuda holds that Rabbi Yehoshua deems one who does first liable, since his mind was to pick both; what difference does it make to me whether he did this one first or that one? And Rabbi Yehoshua said to him: According to your reasoning, if so, why is “wherein he has sinned” stated? Rather, to exclude one who acts unawares and does the later one first, who is exempt. But with ordinary acting unawares on Shabbat, all agree he is exempt.
rashi:a7.1: But isn’t it taught: a support, that we are concerned about what is earlier and what is later.
gershom:a7.1: But isn’t it taught: a support, for we find a baraita that is precise about doing the later one first.
rashi:a7.2: To light this one: in unwitting error about Shabbat or about the labors.
rashi:a7.3: And he lit that one, he is exempt: for that is acting unawares; he intended only one and did not do it, but did the other.
gershom:a8.1: As it is taught: If there were two lamps before him, lit, or two that were out, and with the lit ones he intended to extinguish this one first on Shabbat and extinguished the other one first, or with those that were out he intended to light this one first and lit the other one first, he is liable [our printed baraita reads “exempt”], since they are one category: with lighting we do not mind, and whichever he does first, he is liable; and likewise extinguishing, which is one category, whichever he does first, he is liable. But if there were two, one lit and one out, which is two categories, and he intended to light first, and instead, without intending it, he first extinguished, and with that same extinguishing he lit the other in one breath, for example with the same blowing with which he extinguished this one the flame went and lit the other, he is liable, for that lighting was not later than the extinguishing, since they were in one breath, and his thought was carried out. But with two breaths, where he extinguished this one first with one blowing and lit the other with a second blowing, now that it was with two breaths the lighting is later, and therefore he is exempt. “And with one breath he is liable: is this not obvious?” etc.
rashi:a7.4: To light and to extinguish: when one lamp was lit and one lamp was out, and he intended to light this one first and afterward extinguish that one, and he extinguished this one and afterward lit that one.
rashi:a7.5: If with one breath: he blew, and through the blowing he extinguished this one and lit it [the other]; he is liable, for one cannot say which was earlier and which was later.
rashi:a8.1: With two breaths, he is exempt: for it was not done in order.
rashi:a8.2: His thought was not carried out: for one could say that he extinguished and afterward lit.
gershom:a9.1: It teaches us: since he extinguished and lit with one breath, granted that the lighting was not earlier, it was not later either; rather, he extinguished and lit at once, [with one breath,] and therefore he is liable.
rashi:a9.1: One who stokes [ha-ḥoteh]: one who fills vessels from the pile of coals.
rashi:a9.2: He extinguishes the upper ones: which now become the lower ones and go out because of the weight of the upper ones; and he ignites the lower ones, which had been out because of the weight that was on them, and now that they are the upper ones they are kindled.
rashi:a9.3: What is the reason of the one who imposes two? He did not intend one of them, and with respect to it he is acting unawares.
gershom:a10.1: One who stokes coals on Shabbat: who takes them from one place with a coal pan and puts them in another place. “Liable for two”:
gershom:a11.1: One, because he extinguishes the upper ones: the coals, when he puts them on the ground.
gershom:a12.1: And he ignites the lower ones: those that were earlier the lower ones and dim have now become the upper ones and glowing, and that is igniting.
rashi:a10.1: In order to ignite the lower ones: that is, he did not need the igniting of the lower ones; rather, the extinguishing of the upper ones was his main intention, for he was a smith and needed charcoal. He intended to extinguish the upper ones, which were large, and although he knew that the lower ones would be ignited, he intended the extinguishing of these on the understanding that those would be ignited, even though for him he is ruining them.
tosafot:a10.1: Where he intended to extinguish the upper ones in order to ignite the lower ones: as Rabbi Yoḥanan explains, “They taught it of a nappaḥ.” This is not a smith who blows [the fire]; rather, it means the one who makes charcoal in the forest (Tosafot adds an Old French gloss): the wood burns and becomes charcoal, and he removes the charcoal high off the fire and wants it to go out, to do their work with it, to make iron. And the coals that are small he does not want for warming himself, only that they become ash; and that is a destructive act, since they are fit for nothing, and he would want them to be consumed entirely and become ash. That is “he intended to extinguish the upper ones in order to ignite the lower ones”: that igniting of the lower ones he does not want except that they become ash, and that is a destructive act. According to Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi (Yitzḥak) [Tzadok] he is liable for two, for extinguishing and for kindling, even though it is destructive and even though it is a labor not necessary for its own sake; in this he holds like Rabbi Yehuda, who imposes liability, although he holds like Rabbi Shimon on a destructive act of kindling. And according to the Rabbis he is not liable for kindling, since one who is destructive in kindling is exempt.
rashi:a10.2: Destructive in kindling: as with a smith, as Rabbi Yoḥanan said, “They taught it of a smith,” for a smith does not want the coals to be kindled.
rashi:a10.3: Destructive in kindling, he is liable: for we hold that although others who are destructive are exempt, one who wounds and one who kindles are liable.
gershom:a13.1: Where he intended to extinguish the upper ones: which are large charcoals and valuable for the needs of smiths, and so he puts them on the ground so that they go out; and to ignite the lower ones, which earlier were [below], so that now they are the upper ones, and he intends that they all burn to ash, since they are small coals and he does not care about them. For the first tanna, who imposes only one, holds that one who is destructive in kindling, ruining by burning the coals to ash, is exempt.
gershom:a14.1: And Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the daf reads Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok] holds that one who is destructive in kindling is liable. And so said Rabbi Yoḥanan: “We learned it of a smith,” saying it like Rabbi Ḥanina and Rabbi Elazar, where he intended to extinguish the upper ones, that is, for a smith’s needs. Rabbi Yirmeya [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the daf reads Rabbi Yoḥanan] said: Until here, until Rabbi Yoḥanan interpreted that they taught it of a smith, the reason for this halakha was not revealed: why does Rabbi Elazar impose two?
rashi:a11.1: Ami bar Avin, etc.: where he intended both the extinguishing and the kindling, and even so he is exempt for the kindling, for the first tanna holds like Rabbi Yosei, who said kindling was singled out as a negative prohibition, and there is no offering.
gershom:a15.1: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Ḥanina [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the daf reads Ami bar Avin and Rav Ḥananya bar Avin] both say: where he intended to extinguish and to kindle, he is liable for two; and the first tanna, who imposes only one, holds like Rabbi Yosei, who said kindling was singled out as a negative prohibition and not for a sin offering.
gershom:b1.1: And Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok holds like Rabbi Natan, who said it was singled out to divide, and one is liable for it a sin offering. And some say: until here the reason for this halakha was not revealed, until Abaye bar Avin and Rav Ḥanina bar Avin explained it.
rashi:b3.1: Doing first is the difference between them: where he intended to kindle first and afterward to extinguish, and he kindled and extinguished with one stoking. The first tanna is concerned about earlier and later; therefore he cannot be held liable for two, since perhaps he extinguished first; nor can he be exempted from everything, for granted it was not done earlier, it was not done later either; therefore he is liable for one. And Rabbi Eliezer is not concerned about earlier and later; therefore he is liable for two.
gershom:b2.1: Rava said: Doing first is the difference between them, between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok: where he intended to extinguish first, and he extinguished and ignited at once. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that since his thought was not carried out, as he did not extinguish first, he is exempt for the extinguishing and liable for the kindling; and Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok holds that he is liable for two, for granted that the extinguishing was not earlier, it was not later either.
rashi:b4.1: Rav Ashi said: where he intended to extinguish, and not to kindle, for he did not know that the lower ones would end up kindled.
tosafot:b4.1: He holds like Rabbi Yehuda, who said that one who commits an unintentional act is liable: In brief: Tosafot ask: according to the Ri in the first chapter of Ketubot (5[b]), Rabbi Yehuda forbids an unintentional act only by rabbinic law and not by Torah law, yet here he imposes a sin offering, which is Torah law. They answer that here Rabbi Yehuda imposes liability because it is a pesik reisha [an inevitable consequence]. They ask: if so, even Rabbi Shimon would agree, so how can the first tanna be said to hold like Rabbi Shimon? They answer that the reason here is that it is a labor not necessary for its own sake, on which Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon follow their own views; mentioning an unintentional act was not needed, since it is in any case a labor not necessary for its own sake, and it is also called unintentional because he does not want the coals kindled and derives no benefit from them. In the baraita of one who stokes coals to be warmed by them, intent is not at issue, since he does it to be warmed; but it is a labor not necessary for its own sake, so Rabbi Shimon exempts though it is a pesik reisha. They ask from chapter HaBoneh (Shabbat 103a), where the Gemara says “even say in land that is not a marsh,” since it is unintentional and exempt like Rabbi Shimon, and objects from Abaye and Rava, who both say that Rabbi Shimon concedes with a pesik reisha: why object, if in any case it is a labor not necessary for its own sake? They answer that there it was first assumed to be a pesik reisha that pleases him, so it answers that he does it in another’s land, a pesik reisha that does not please him. The Arukh likewise brings that a pesik reisha that does not please one is permitted, from Sukka 33b: one may reduce [the berries] in the lulav on the festival; the Gemara objects that he is fixing it, and answers that he has another hoshana, or that it is not necessary for its own sake, and even though he fixes it, it is permitted. [See also Tosafot Shabbat 41b, s.v. meiḥam.] Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b3.1: Where he intended to extinguish, and they went out, and they ignited by themselves: the first tanna holds like Rabbi Shimon, who said that an unintentional act is exempt, as we learned: “Rabbi Shimon says: A person may drag a bed,” etc.
gershom:b4.1: And Rabbi Elazar [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text] holds like Rabbi Yehuda, who said that an unintentional act is forbidden, as he says regarding a firstborn: even if it would die, one does not let its blood, because he holds that even an unintentional act is forbidden.
rashi:b5.1: Not necessary for its own sake: such as this one, who does not need to kindle them, only to be warmed by stoking them; in any case he knew that they would be kindled and did it on that understanding, so he is acting with intent; but this kindling is a labor not necessary for its own sake.
gershom:b5.1: That which is taught “liable” holds that one is liable for a labor not necessary for its own sake: for the usual way with coals is only to roast meat, and this one, although he stoked them for warmth and not for roasting, and they ignited, is liable. And the other tanna holds that one is exempt for a labor not necessary for its own sake; and moreover, they ignited by themselves.
rashi:b7.1: Mishna. One consumed blood of slaughter of an animal: whether of a domesticated animal, of an undomesticated animal, or of birds.
tosafot:b7.1: One consumed blood of slaughter, etc.: In brief: The Ri asked: the Gemara expounds, “just as an animal, an undomesticated animal and a bird impart severe impurity and light impurity,” yet a non-kosher bird does not render clothing impure in the place of swallowing, and so does not impart severe impurity; from where, then, do we know that its blood is forbidden? One can say that by the conclusion it is resolved, since it is derived through a general rule and a detail, and this is what it means: “of bird or of animal”: just as bird and animal are distinguished in that within their species there is severe and light impurity, as with the kosher ones, excluding fish and grasshoppers, in whose species there is no severe impurity at all. So too one must explain “and they have prohibition and permission,” which is explained later (Keritot 21b) as a prohibition before slaughter and a permission after slaughter: otherwise, for a non-kosher bird or animal, which have no permission after slaughter, from where would it know? Rather, it means that within the species of animal and bird there is prohibition and permission; and even according to the one who says that slaughter of birds is not from the Torah, at least stabbing is required, so there is prohibition and permission. Prohibition and permission could also be explained as a prohibition before death, of a limb from a living creature, and a permission after death; but regarding severe impurity one must explain as above. And in the Gemara, where it says, “if, just as an animal, to which [the law of] the mother with the young does not apply, so too a bird,” etc., it could equally have said, “if, just as an animal that imparts severe impurity, so too a bird,” excluding the blood of a non-kosher bird, which does not impart severe impurity; and it could likewise have explained “a bird to which the mother with the young does not apply” as one that is ready at hand, but not one that is not ready at hand. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:b7.2: Whether blood of stabbing or blood of ripping [ikkur]: where he tore out their signs [the windpipe and gullet].
rashi:b7.3: Or blood of bloodletting with which the soul departs, one is liable for it: karet, since they are the blood of the soul. And in the Gemara it explains which is the blood of bloodletting with which the soul departs.
tosafot:b7.2: Blood of ripping [ikkur]: Some explain blood of ikkur as where the signs were torn out from their place of attachment. But this is difficult: since the animal does not die by that, and it is a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai that it is disqualified, but it is not a tereifa, if so its blood is not subject to karet, since the soul does not depart with it. Therefore one must say: blood of a slaughter that took place after ikkur.
tosafot:b7.3: Blood of bloodletting with which the soul departs: The same applies to blood of slaughter, stabbing and ripping, that we require that the soul depart with it; but it needed to be stated only regarding the blood of bloodletting, since it is not usual to let blood from one’s animal until the blood of the soul comes.
gershom:b7.1: Blood of stabbing: pressing or ripping.
gershom:b8.1: And blood of bloodletting of an animal with which the soul departs: that is, the blood of the spurt; one is liable to karet for it, excluding the blood that trickles at first and at the end.
rashi:b8.1: Blood of eggs [beitzim]: the testicles of a ram or an ox. Another version: blood of addled eggs that turned red from the warmth of the hen sitting on them.
rashi:b8.2: One is not liable for them: karet, for there is karet only for the blood of the soul, as it is written (Leviticus 17:14): “For the life of all flesh is its blood… whoever eats it shall be cut off.”
tosafot:b8.1: Blood of eggs: The Kuntres [Rashi] explained: a hen’s egg; another version: male testicles. [Rashi on our page gives the testicles first and the hen’s eggs as the other version.] But this is difficult, for in the Gemara it says, “I will exclude the blood of eggs, as they are not a type of meat.”
tosafot:b8.2: Blood of fish, one is not liable for it [Tosafot’s text of the mishna lists blood of fish, which our printed mishna does not]: This implies that there is nonetheless a prohibition. But this is difficult, for in the Gemara it says, “Rav said: Blood of fish that one collected is forbidden,” and it raises an objection to him from a baraita; but why not support him from our mishna? One can say: indeed, it could have said so, and [answered], “And according to your reasoning, let the mishna be difficult for it.”
gershom:b9.1: Blood of the (firstborn) [spleen] [the printed text reads “firstborn,” corrected to “spleen”] that left it, and blood of the heart that left it, blood of the beitzim of an animal: one is not liable to karet for them, only for a mere prohibition. And blood of fish, grasshoppers and creeping animals, one is not liable for them, etc., as is explained in the Gemara.
gershom:b10.1: Even the blood of bipeds: such as a person. And the blood of eggs in the baraita refers to eggs of a bird that are addled and mixed with blood.
rashi:b10.1: Gemara. Light impurity: impurity of foods, with an egg-bulk.
rashi:b10.2: Severe impurity: when it is an unslaughtered carcass, it imparts impurity by carrying. And they have a prohibition before slaughter and a permission after slaughter.
tosafot:b10.1: That have severe impurity and light impurity, and have prohibition and permission, and are a type of meat: Rabbeinu Barukh found it difficult: why are all these aspects needed? One of them would suffice, for “I will exclude the blood of bipeds, which have no light impurity”; and likewise the aspect of permission and prohibition would suffice.
gershom:b11.1: Just as bird and animal are distinguished in that they have light impurity: that is, the impurity of foods, with an egg-bulk; and severe impurity, that they impart impurity to a person by carrying, as it is written of them: “And one who carries their carcass.”
gershom:b12.1: And they have a prohibition before slaughter, of eating, and a permission after slaughter.
gershom:b13.1: I will exclude the blood of bipeds, which have no light impurity: for a person does not become impure with the impurity of foods.
